items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: And Louis Hayes does what he does, Max does what he does, Kenny Clarke did what he did, Jo Jones did what he did, Sonny Greer. All of them. Elvin Hayes, Buddy Rich, Gene Krupa.

ctx.x: And active I guess. If you can be real honest, and don’t worry about your ego, can you tell me where do you fit in the line of drummers in innovation and in your music? I mean I don’t know if I asked that question very well but—

Well I don’t know. I’m being very honest. First of all it’s totally impossible for two drummers to play alike, because of the physical aspect. One might have long arms, one might have short arms. And if you have short arms that means that you have to sit closer to your instrument. If you have long arms you sit back, that type of thing, for reach. And just the space between makes a difference in the sound you’re going to get, or the touch you’re going to acquire to get the sound. I don’t sound like anybody else,…
It’s usually left to the non-musicians I guess to try to put down, this guy was influenced by this guy, influenced by this guy, and so forth. Sometimes it’s true and sometimes maybe not.

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Buddy Rich played and them people, they applauded about a half an hour. I mean they went crazy, right. And I had to follow him, my cello group, right and me.

ctx.x: I don’t remember you telling us about that.

It was in LA, man, and there was joint that opened up on the strip, small place, only held about 90 people and Dave Pell and his octet, Buddy Rich Quintet when he had Sweets, and Sonny Chris, my group, and Slim and Slam.
We’re back in -- wow how far back -- we’re going back early ‘50s, late ‘40s? How far back are we going?
